questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to study somewhere, where the culture would be the most different from my home country (Denmark), and so I chose Tokyo. My decision was solely based on what I knew about Tokyo as a city, and therefore not on what the University could offer me.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: All the important information was easy to find through Manaba (the Japanese student portal). There is, however, a lot of bureaucracy regarding student visas etc., but Chuo University also took care of most of that for me. I felt that I had all the information I needed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an introductory meeting when I arrived which contained most of the important stuff. Other than that, it was pretty easy to figure it out on my own.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found it rather easy to find accommodation. We booked an Airbnb for 4 months, where the rent was very fair and the location was central.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I would definitely (!!!) recommend people attending Chuo University Law School to get off campus housing, as the on campus housing is more than 1 hour and 30 minutes away from the law campus. I know that a lot of the other exchange students had good experiences finding off campus housing themselves, but it also seemed like a big advantage to use the on campus housing to meet new people and other students. So, if you are traveling alone, getting on campus housing would probably be nice if you do not ind the long commute.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration of courses was rather difficult, as the course syllabuses were hard to find, and it was not easy to figure out when the classes were held. However, using the Manaba portal was quite intuitive and it is not that big of a hurdle.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The foreign student administration was very helpful to provide me with course syllabuses, so I could plan my classes how I wanted.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I registred for six courses and got all of them, which meant that I only had one full day with classes and two days with only one class each week.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Read the syllabuses for each course and note in which period they are held (MON2, TUE3 etc.). This way, it is possible to plan your courses over 2 or 3 days and have the rest of the week off.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There was sufficient english courses held at Chuo University. There are very few courses on japanese law, and so most of the courses are about human rights, international law etc.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of courses did not match those of a masters student at my home university. The academic level was very different across the different classes, but generally speaking it was definitely lower than that of my home institution - all exchange students felt this way. The law courses was more about policy than the actual study of law. Still, the classes were interesting and some of them provided insight to and knowledge about Japanese culture, history, law etc.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching varied a lot across classes. In some classes, students were expected to participate very actively and in other classes, the teacher spoke for the entire length of the class.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Human Rights Problems in Japan, Comparative Labour and Employment Law, Doing Business in Japan (Advising Clients on Legal Strategy), International Law from Japanese Perspectives, Business and Human Rights, and Introduction to Japanese Law.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I think that Comparative Labour and Employment Law and Doing Business in Japan were two very good classes. They are both taught by an Australian, which makes the academic level of english a bit higher than that of the Japanese professors. Students are expected to participate more actively but that just made the course better. I definitely would also recommend Business and Human Rights, which was a very active participation class as well.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: No unexpected costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Japan is very affordable in general. Food is very cheap and you can easily go out to eat every day on a normal budget. Traveling both in Japan and to other regions of Asia was also cheap. It is definitely a lot cheaper to go to Japan than a lot of other exchange destinations, so I would not worry about this.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a couple of gatherings and parties but not a lot. It is, however, very easy to make new friends on exchange and to set up social gatherings with them. Also, Chuo provides a lot of athletic activities, such as martial arts, basketball etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Travel around Japan and Asie and experience the culture outside of Tokyo. During our stay we had time to travel through a lot of Japan as well as China, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam. Definitely use this opportunity to see as much of Japan (and Asia) as possible.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Public transportation is very easy and affordable, so I would recommend visiting different parts of Tokyo and to research what events might take place while you are there. Also, travel Japan and Asia.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It is definitely a "culture shock" to visit Japan for the first time. However, it is very easy to get a grasp of the local norms and culture. People are a lot more friendly to foreigners than expected and overall it was just a great experience to encounter such a different culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It is difficult to socialize with the local students, as most Japanese people's english skills are bad or non existing. I imagine it would be easier, if you speak Japanese, but the vast majority of exchange students socialized with other exchange students - not local students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It can be challenging not to speak Japanese in Japan, as most Japanese people do not speak english, and as workers at most restaurants, bars etc. only speak Japanese. While this might be challenging to begin with, Japanese people are very friendly and accommodating, and I found it to be no hurdle at all.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Japan is a wonderful country with rich culture. I really appreciated their warmth and welcomeness towards foreign exchange students - I did not expect this. The food was fantastic, Tokyo was a vibrant and colorful city, and the nature outside of Tokyo is marvelous.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Do not get intimidated by all the bureaucracy - this is completely normal in Japan, and you will get through it. Socialize with the other exchange students - go to dinners, drinks, sport events etc. Travel Japan outside of Tokyo - there is so much more.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Learn basic Japanese phrases - that will get you far.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To experience Japan as a country and to meet new friends from across the world. Japan is a fantastic country and if you are in doubt, go! Would definitely recommend going there to anyone, it is an experience for life.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The bureaucracy of trying to register my address - took me six hours. Apart from this, I think my stay had very few challenges worthy of mention - it was just a great experience overall.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
